title: What's poopy about a poop deck? | NAUTICAL ETYMOLOGY

entries.note: Greek for ship, the source of many English words connected with sailing, such as [[gave:nausea]] and [[gave:navicular]].
Greek for sailor, from [[from:naus]], and the source of [[gave:nautical]].
Comes from Greek [[from:nautes]], sailor.
Given as an example of a word from the same ship root as [[same-root:nautical]].
Given as an example of a word from the same ship root as [[same-root:nautical]].
Means boat-shaped and comes from the same ship root as [[same-root:nautical]].
The feeling that you are going to vomit; it literally means seasickness or ship sickness, from [[from:naus]].
Describes something repeated until it becomes tiresome; it literally means to the point of being sick, specifically seasick, like [[same-root:nausea]].
Literally star sailor; Rob calls it the cutest etymology in English.
The Russian counterpart of [[see:astronaut]], literally a cosmos sailor.
Built on the idea of an air sailor, from the same sailor root as [[same-root:astronaut]].
The mythological sailors of Jason who sailed on the Argo, given as another -naut word.
The famous boat from [[see:20,000 Leagues Under the Sea]]; its name is basically a poetic form of the Greek word for sailor.
Nothing to do with stars: it comes from an old Germanic steer board, the side where early boats carried their single rudder.
Replaced [[from:larboard]]; probably linked to [[same-root?:portal]] and [[same-root?:porthole]] as the entry side for loading, rather than the docking side.
The old opposite of [[see:starboard]], probably from a loading board related to German laden and English [[same-root:load]]; it was dropped because it sounded too similar.
Related to German laden, to load, which may explain [[same-root:larboard]] as the loading side.
Etymologists more often link it to [[same-root?:port]], with the shared idea of an entry point.
Mentioned as related to [[same-root?:port]], since the port side was where cargo was loaded through holes.
Contrasted with a [[see:port]], which is an entry point, while a harbour is where you actually stop.
The front of a boat, paired with [[see:aft]].
The back of a boat, paired with [[see:fore]].
The back of a boat, named after steering, because later boats were steered from the back.
The front of a boat, possibly from an old Germanic word for shoulders, which would make it related to [[same-root?:bough]].
A tree's arms or shoulders, spelled differently but possibly related to [[same-root?:bow]].
Comes from judging an approaching boat by the shape of its [[from:jib]], which differed from country to country.
A triangular sail at the front of a boat, whose shape could show where a ship came from.
Spelled with toe, not tow: British naval seamen lined up for inspection with their toes against the seams of the deck.
Gossip; originally the sailors' water-cooler talk around a [[from:butt]] of drinking water with a [[from:scuttle]], or hole, in its top.
A cask of fresh drinking water aboard a ship, which gave [[gave:scuttlebutt]].
A hole in the top of a cask; to scuttle a boat is to sink it on purpose by making a hole in it.
Supposedly nautical: a sail taken [[from:aback]] has been blown backwards against the structure holding it up.
Simply means backwards; one of many nautical words with the [[from:a-]] prefix.
A Germanic prefix from Old English meaning in or onto; Jess thinks it survives in so many nautical words because seafaring was central to British culture.
An example of a nautical word with the [[see:a-]] prefix.
An example of a nautical word with the [[see:a-]] prefix.
An example of a Germanic word with the [[see:a-]] prefix.
An example of a Germanic word with the [[see:a-]] prefix.
An example of a Germanic word with the [[see:a-]] prefix.
An example of a Germanic word with the [[see:a-]] prefix.
Refers to [[from:tacking]], zigzagging into the wind; changing tack means changing direction so you can keep moving forward.
Sailing into the wind by zigzagging and changing direction, which gave [[gave:take a different tack]].
Colours are flags: deceptive ships flew a friendly nation's flag, then hoisted their real one once battle began.
The pirate flag; jolly once meant gallant, as in [[see:jolly Robin]], and the origin of [[see:roger]] is debated.
An old term for a handsome, charming, gallant man, showing the older sense of jolly in [[see:Jolly Roger]].
Possibly linked to large things or to an old verb meaning to beat violently; in British slang, to roger means to have sex.
Implies taking by force, but probably first meant baggage, clothes or household goods, so plunder was simply the goods taken.
The common name for the UK's flag; pedants prefer [[see:Union flag]], since a [[see:jack]] is flown from a boat, but Rob sees it as a proper name now.
A flag flown from a boat, which is why some object to calling the UK flag the [[see:Union Jack]] on land.
The name pedants insist on for the [[see:Union Jack]] when it isn't flown from a boat.
Pirate loot, a bottom and sex all come from one source, a Middle English word for plunder taken from an enemy, via Old French from Germanic.
An emphatic phrase implying an advantage, with the same sense found in the source of [[same-root:booty]].
Lasted roughly from the 1650s to the 1750s; most of the 'pirate' terms and the accent came later, from pop culture.
The pirate from [[see:Treasure Island]] whose phrasing gave [[see:shiver me timbers]], and whose film portrayal by [[see:Robert Newton]] shaped the pirate accent.
The author of [[see:Treasure Island]], who gave us many pirate terms and ideas such as [[see:walking the plank]].
One of the pirate ideas we owe to [[see:Robert Louis Stevenson]] rather than to real pirates of the golden age.
Played [[see:Long John Silver]] in a 1950s Treasure Island adaptation; his Cornish accent and 'arr' became the stereotypical pirate voice.
An iconic novel that romanticised the golden age of piracy and popularised many pirate phrases.
The Spanish silver dollar, worth eight reales and used by British colonists short of currency; a [[see:piece]] meant a coin, though some say they were cut into eight.
Here means a coin, which explains [[see:pieces of eight]].
A Spanish currency unit; the Spanish silver dollar, or [[see:pieces of eight]], was worth eight reales.
American slang for a quarter dollar: two one-real pieces cut from a piece of eight, a quarter of its value; from [[from:pieces of eight]].
Spanish in origin, reaching English through French; it means a double, a gold coin worth twice another Spanish coin, perhaps the [[see:pistole]].
Jess thinks this was the Spanish gold coin that a [[see:doubloon]] was worth twice as much as.
A golden-age pirate term short for [[from:hold fast]], possibly shaped by the Dutch version; it means stop or hold steady, and is now a general pirate interjection.
The phrase that [[gave:avast]] is short for.
The Old English word for a pirate, used before the word [[see:pirate]] existed.
The Old English way of saying pirate ship.
One of the Old English compounds the hosts love for the sea.
Another Old English compound for the sea, alongside [[see:hwælweg]].
An Old English poem in which an old mariner reflects on his life and on his passage to the afterlife as his next voyage.
Someone paid by a country to plunder; first meant a privately owned armed ship, then its sailors, following [[see:buccaneer]]; [[see:Francis Drake]] is the most famous example.
Probably the most famous [[see:privateer]], who sailed on behalf of Queen Elizabeth I.
Basically the Greek word for a pirate, meaning someone who attacks; it didn't exist in Old English.
Literally one who roasts meat on a [[from:boucan]]; the word is specific to the Caribbean.
A grill used by the Tupi people of what is now Brazil, which gave [[gave:buccaneer]].
A pirate of the Mediterranean, from a tense period of clashes at sea between Muslims and Christians; Jess wonders whether it relates to [[same-root?:Corsica]].
Jess wonders whether it is related to [[same-root?:Corsair]] because the words look so similar.
In the 1500s, any swaggering sword fighter carrying a [[from:swash]] weapon and a [[from:buckler]]; later bombastic military types, a bit like [[see:chauvinist]]s.
The heavy blow of a weapon, the first part of [[gave:swashbuckler]].
A shield, the second part of [[gave:swashbuckler]].
Compared with [[see:swashbuckler]], a later word for people who made their identity about military bombast.
A pirate favourite; it is not land lover or land liver but contains [[from:lubber]], a large, clumsy or idle person.
A large, clumsy, unintelligent or idle person, used mainly of lazy monks; you could be a lubber anywhere, not just on land.
The laziest monk in the abbey, a use of [[see:lubber]].
An idiom from some 500 or 600 years ago, built on [[see:lubber]].
A fictional plant that made people lazy; Rob jokes that today it might be called cannabis.
A mythical land of pleasant idleness, similar to the folk songs' [[see:Big Rock Candy Mountain]].
A paradise from folk songs, compared with [[see:Lubberland]].
Refers to wooden ships splintering in rough seas, from [[from:shiver]]; popularised by [[see:Long John Silver]] but recorded in a 1795 publication.
A small piece, fragment or splinter, especially of a smashed ship, which gave [[gave:shiver me timbers]].
A deck at the [[from:poop]] of a ship, a term that always raises a snigger.
Said here to be the frontmost part of a boat, though it comes from Latin [[from:puppis]], which also meant the stern.
One of many ship parts named with [[see:poop]].
One of many ship parts named with [[see:poop]].
One of many ship parts named with [[see:poop]].
One of many ship parts named with [[see:poop]].
Not a figurehead but a cruel term for a useless apprentice, who might as well have been inanimate.
Drunk: three [[from:sheet]]s, or ropes, loose in the wind meant the sails were out of control, like a drunken sailor.
On a ship, a rope rather than a sail, as you might expect, which explains [[see:three sheets to the wind]].
Later than the golden age; probably from [[from:wag]] and [[from?:scall]] or [[from?:Scalloway]], for poor emigrants. In the American South it meant white opponents of the Confederacy.
A back-and-forth motion, also wavering or lacking steadfastness; a wag was a disreputable rascal or a mischievous child.
Called a Scottish word and a possible source of [[gave?:scalawag]]; Rob says it survives as unkind English slang.
A clock with an open pendulum, named after its [[see:wag]].
Someone destined to swing from the gallows, a use of [[see:wag]].
In Shetland; its poor emigrants to America in the 1800s may have been the first [[see:scalawag]]s.
The wave of the sea came from [[from:waw]], reshaped by the unrelated hand wave, which is related to [[same-root:waggle]].
The old word for a wave on water, later reshaped into [[gave:wave]]; Jess wonders whether it imitated the sound or motion of waves.
As in a dog's tail, related to the hand [[same-root:wave]] through the idea of oscillating motion.
Linked with pirates by Pirates of the Caribbean; from the golden-age era, a slangy adaptation of French [[from:savez-vous]], do you know.
The French phrase adapted into [[gave:savvy]].
Discussed in an earlier episode on the telephone greeting; it comes from a Dutch word.
From ropes tied to a [[from:bitt]] on deck; reaching the bitt end meant running out of rope; link to [[unrelated:bitter]] is probably folk etymology.
A fixture on a boat that a rope's end was tied to, which gave [[gave:the bitter end]].
The taste word, apparently unrelated to [[unrelated:the bitter end]], though people have infused the phrase with its sense.
The work that features the boat [[see:Nautilus]].
